A Streetcar Named Desire. Tennessee Williams' 1947 play depicts the collision between Blanche DuBois, a fading Southern belle seeking refuge with her sister in New Orleans, and her brother-in-law Stanley Kowalski, a crude, brutish working man. The clash of refinement and raw physicality, combined with Blanche's precarious mental state, builds to a catastrophic ending.

The play won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1948 and became a cornerstone of American realism. The 1951 film adaptation was equally acclaimed. Blanche arrives at her sister's cramped apartment with secrets—she lost her plantation home and has been drifting as a schoolteacher and sex worker. Stanley's discovery of Blanche's past drives her further into delusion. He ultimately rapes her, an act the play handles with shocking directness.

The play's most famous line is Blanche's desperate cry as she is taken away to a mental institution: "I have always depended on the kindness of strangers." The streetcar named Desire is a literal New Orleans transit line, but it functions as a symbol of inescapable fate and base human appetite. Williams uses Southern Gothic imagery—decay, sensuality, madness—to dissect the gap between illusion and reality.

Tennessee Williams created his exploration of desire, fragility, and the Southern psyche. The character of Stanley Kowalski represents the brute force that shatters Blanche's constructed world. Southern Gothic is the aesthetic and literary tradition Williams embodies. Death of a Salesman similarly dissects post-war American disillusionment and mental collapse. And The Glass Menagerie, Williams' other major work, similarly explores memory, illusion, and a woman undone by reality.
